This is a reply from Council Member A.

Everything below is based on public information: no cloning or deployment. Anything labelled ‘unverified’ remains for local CORE_06-0a verification.

Your added requirements change this selection's target: 3 repos ultimately, with stronger holdout confidentiality. So I recommend screening **3 main candidates plus 1 backup**, rather than just 2–3. Section 8 discusses this separately.

---

## 1–2. Candidate pool and URLs

| # | Candidate | Structure | Licence | Maintenance | Third-party authentication | Fame risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | RealWorld: Angular frontend + ASP.NET Core backend | 2 repos | MIT | Active | None (local JWT) | Extremely high |
| C2 | Spring PetClinic: REST backend + Angular frontend | 2 repos | Apache-2.0 | Active | None; no registration either | High |
| C3 | Full Stack FastAPI Template | Single repo (separate frontend/ and backend/) | MIT | Active (exact date unverified) | Optional SMTP | Extremely high |
| C4 | ivangfr/springboot-react-keycloak | Single repo | **LICENSE not found** | Unverified | Keycloak + OMDb key + optional Google/GitHub IdP | Medium-low |
| C5 | mortogo321/spring-angular-sso | Single repo, separate frontend/backend Dockerfiles | MIT | Very new, few commits | Keycloak PKCE | Almost zero |
| C6 | GCP three-tier Terraform solution + application repo | 2 repos (IaC + app) | Apache-2.0 | Unverified | None | Medium |

**URLs:**
- C1: `github.com/realworld-apps/angular-realworld-example-app`, `github.com/realworld-apps/aspnetcore-realworld-example-app` (spec: `realworld-apps/realworld`)
- C2: `github.com/spring-petclinic/spring-petclinic-angular`, `github.com/spring-petclinic/spring-petclinic-rest`
- C3: `github.com/fastapi/full-stack-fastapi-template`
- C4: `github.com/ivangfr/springboot-react-keycloak`
- C5: `github.com/mortogo321/spring-angular-sso`
- C6: `github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/terraform-google-three-tier-web-app`, `github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/deploystack-three-tier-app`

## 3–5. Each candidate: licence, maintenance, Docker, acceptance leads and risks

**C1 RealWorld**
- Maintenance: moved to the realworld-apps organisation. ASP.NET Core backend (MIT) last updated 2026-09-02; Angular frontend 2026-08-04.
- Acceptance: backend CI runs the official RealWorld API specification tests (Hurl and Bruno), usable against an already-running server. This is the most objective acceptance method among the 6 candidates.
- Frontend: MIT, Bun build, Playwright configuration in the repo. No Dockerfile seen at root (unverified), so AI needs to containerise it, without business-code changes.
- **The biggest risk is the public-demo trap, and it really exists:** the official live demo still operates at demo.realworld.show. If the frontend defaults to the public API, a misconfigured deployment can appear functional, directly matching §8.2 item 2. It is a useful experimental trap, but its existence must first be confirmed locally.
- Database: SQLite by default, also SQL Server (source: a mirror README claiming to copy the official repo). Persistence after restart depends on volume mounting, another useful trap.
- Highest fame risk; the model may have memorised deployment. No third-party authentication either.

**C2 Spring PetClinic**
- Maintenance: REST backend Apache-2.0, updated 2026-09-01; frontend upgraded to Angular 22, updated 2026-08-06.
- Docker: frontend has a Dockerfile; backend defaults to in-memory HSQLDB, with MySQL and PostgreSQL configurations too. Data is not persistent by default, a natural trap.
- Acceptance: Postman/Newman regression tests.
- **Major flaw:** no user registration or login; §8.2 item 4 cannot be met unchanged, so acceptance must be rewritten. Keep it as backup.

**C3 Full Stack FastAPI Template**
- Maintenance: MIT, active repository; exact date unverified.
- CI and secrets best match your requirements: GitHub Actions deploys to staging and production through environment-labelled self-hosted runners. Documentation explicitly lists workflow secrets; SECRET_KEY, FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD and POSTGRES_PASSWORD must change before deployment, preferably through secrets. This directly tests F7 (record secret locations, not values).
- Acceptance: frontend Playwright e2e (unverified).
- Risks:
  - Defaults to separate dashboard, api and adminer subdomains. Each run needs several manual Cloudflare records, adding human gates.
  - Complete deployment.md makes it ‘easy mode’.
  - Extremely high fame and single repo.

**C4 ivangfr springboot-react-keycloak (not recommended)**
- Requires OMDb API key and Java 25; Google/GitHub IdP integration relies on the author's Medium article.
- No LICENSE in the file listing. It cannot enter publicly reported experiments before confirmation. Frontend still starts as a dev server.

**C5 mortogo321 spring-angular-sso**
- Structure: MIT, one compose orchestrates five services: postgres, keycloak, keycloak-init, backend and frontend; login uses Keycloak PKCE.
- CI pushes images to GHCR; the deployment job exists but is commented out and requires DEPLOY_HOST, DEPLOY_USER and DEPLOY_SSH_KEY secrets. Also a manually triggered rollback workflow.
- **A real deployment trap:** Keycloak issuer is fixed to localhost:8081; backend token checks require an exact issuer match. Live deployment needs issuer reconfiguration, without code changes. This tests ‘works locally ≠ works remotely’.
- Risks:
  - Only 9 commits and 0 stars, one maintainer, liable to change or disappear. Pin commit SHA or save a snapshot.
  - Nobody has reviewed code quality.
  - Keycloak plus two JVM services may increase VM memory/specification and cost (unverified).

**C6 GCP three-tier Terraform application (reference only)**
- Frontend deployed to two Cloud Run services; Go API also uses Cloud Run, with Memorystore Redis cache, Cloud SQL database and Cloud Build.
- The only candidate among the 6 with ready IaC, but:
  - Serverless, so §8.2 item 5 (data survives VM restart) does not apply.
  - No user authentication.
  - Memorystore and Cloud SQL have minimum fixed costs.
  - The task would essentially become running `terraform apply` once.

## 6. Candidates recommended for CORE_06-0a

**Main: C1, C3, C5. Backup: C2.**

These complement one another:
- **C1:** most objective acceptance, genuinely separate frontend/backend and a real public-API trap.
- **C3:** fullest CI / GitHub Secrets requirements, medium complexity.
- **C5:** Keycloak authentication, real issuer trap, almost zero fame.

C2 replaces a main candidate only if screening fails.

## 7. Unknowns needing local verification

- **C1:**
  - Default frontend API address: does it point to the public demo? How is API URL changed at build time?
  - Does the backend have a Dockerfile?
  - SQLite path and persistence; CORS configuration.
  - Can Hurl/Bruno tests pass against containerised services?
- **C3:**
  - Is registration enabled by default?
  - Is a self-hosted runner on the VM feasible?
  - Is Traefik certificate issuance compatible with Cloudflare proxy mode?
  - Do Playwright tests exist and pass?
- **C5:**
  - Last commit date.
  - Production issuer and KC_HOSTNAME configuration paths.
  - Does the Keycloak realm allow self-registration?
  - Whole-stack memory use and feasibility on a small VM.
  - Selected commit SHA.
- **C2:**
  - Is Angular's API address hard-coded?
  - Can the PostgreSQL profile be switched directly?

Confirm every candidate's actual licence file and check every ‘X is absent’ conclusion. Under v1.7, these negative conclusions require positive controls.

---

## 8. Your three-repository plan and requirements to narrow

**I support the three-repository plan; it is fairer than the original roadmap.**

Original §7: Run A on development repo, design WatchOver around the exposed problems, then Run B on that same development repo. WatchOver would overfit it, inherently favouring WatchOver in A/B.

Your plan: design sees only repo1's blind-test evidence; A/B uses repo2, unseen during design; repo3 is final holdout. This is cleaner.

Three costs must enter roadmap v0.2:

- **Cost:** one extra bare run. With a $40 fuse per run, 4 runs worst-case cost $160 and 5 cost $200, both within $280. But Run C (Guarded) largely no longer fits, so explicitly remove or downgrade it.
- **Confidentiality:** Council has now seen the whole candidate pool. If exactly 3 are screened and 3 selected, holdout cannot be secret. Screen 4; you privately assign slots, and design sessions receive only repo1 evidence. The Reviewer must also check skills for workload-specific rules, such as hard-coded Keycloak issuer handling.
- **Order within repo2:** whether Bare AI or WatchOver runs first, you as Observer learn from the first. With n=1, counterbalancing is impossible; record order as a known confounder.

This changes roadmap §4/§7, not Frozen Truth (F9 still holds). Council approval and a designated merge owner for a v0.2 patch are needed.

**I suggest narrowing two requirements.** Scope is expanding this round, so I will be strict here.

- **Ready Terraform/Pulumi:** usable GCP IaC reduces bare AI's task to one apply, reducing space for WatchOver to show a difference. AWS IaC instead creates a major porting task. You actually want to test secrets and CI governance; C3/C5 already cover that. C6 stays reference-only.
- **Google auth:** tied to your personal Google account, requiring consent screen, client secret and real-domain redirects. This is not reproducible between runs and brings your personal account into the experiment. In-stack Keycloak is deterministic. Google IdP should be optional for repo3 at most.

Also define equivalent acceptance separately per repository for §8.2 items 3 and 4, particularly what ‘registration’ means in Keycloak. Freeze these before Run A.

This is a reply from Council Member C.

---

### 1. Core preliminary checks and experiment-method calibration (on the Human Operator's proposal)

Before the candidate pool, calibrate two key proposals against PROJECT_ROADMAP v0.1 and Council Constitution v1.7:

1. **A/B attribution requires Run A and Run B to use exactly the same Workload.**


* Roadmap §3 and §7 are frozen: **main A/B/C experiments all use the same Dev Workload**. Different repositories for Run A (bare AI) and Run B (initial WatchOver) would completely contaminate differences with ‘technology stack, dependency traps and code quality’, undermining the methodology for WatchOver effectiveness.


* **Therefore, 3 repositories for three evolution rounds are unnecessary; only 2 are needed:**


* **Dev Workload:** Run A (bare-AI baseline), Run B (WatchOver Basic), Run C (WatchOver Guarded).


* **Holdout Workload:** final generalisation test after the tool takes shape (Run H), strictly secret from the tool-building session until Phase 3.






2. **Beware ‘scope consumption’ by third-party authentication (Keycloak / Google Auth) and existing IaC:**
* **Keycloak** needs at least 1.5–2GB RAM (JVM), complex Realm configuration, Client Secret and precise Redirect URI matching. With one VM, US$280 and a hard 31-day window, bare AI could get stuck in JVM OOM or Keycloak CORS troubleshooting, exhausting the 4-hour fuse.


* **Google Auth** requires manual Google Cloud Console creation of an OAuth 2.0 Client ID and authorised domains; pure CLI/automated deployment acceptance is impossible, disrupting the objective benchmark.
* **Existing Terraform/Pulumi/CI-CD:** WatchOver is designed as a deployment orchestration workbench (Stage 01-04). Highly customised built-in IaC may cause AI to ‘run existing scripts’ rather than establish deployment state, preventing an effective test of WatchOver's architecture planning and state management.


* **Best balance:** decoupled architecture with ‘built-in DB-based authentication (JWT/Session), environment-variable injection (Secret Tokens), native Docker Compose support and no specific cloud binding’.





---

### 2. Candidate combinations (5)

| # | Combination | Stack (FE / BE / DB) | Decoupling | Licence / maintenance | Recommended role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **C1** | **RealWorld Classic** | React 18 + Node/Express + MongoDB/Postgres | Two independent repos | MIT / active community maintenance (updated this year) | Dev backup (classic baseline) |
| **C2** | **RealWorld Modern** | Vue 3 (Vite) + FastAPI + PostgreSQL | Two independent repos | MIT / stable (maintained 2024–2025) | **First Dev choice** |
| **C3** | **RealWorld Ultra-Light** | SvelteKit + Golang (Gin) + SQLite/Postgres | Two independent repos | MIT / stable | **First Holdout choice** |
| **C4** | **Vikunja (open-source task system)** | Vue 3 (TS) + Go + PostgreSQL/MySQL | Genuinely decoupled two repos | AGPL-3.0 / frequent active maintenance | Real-project comparison backup |
| **C5** | **RealWorld Enterprise** | Angular + Spring Boot 3 + PostgreSQL | Two independent repos | MIT / maintained | Stress-test backup |

---

### 3. Detailed candidate analysis

#### C1: RealWorld React + Node Express

* **Frontend**: `[https://github.com/gothinkster/react-redux-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/gothinkster/react-redux-realworld-example-app)`
* **Backend**: `[https://github.com/gothinkster/node-express-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/gothinkster/node-express-realworld-example-app)`
* **Initial licence and maintenance:** MIT. Official RealWorld benchmark implementation, periodic dependency upgrades, mature maintenance.
* **Docker/Compose and acceptance leads:**
* Backend generally has a basic Dockerfile, typically supports local Node or Docker startup.
* Complete RealWorld Postman/Newman API automation tests; objective acceptance through `APIURL`.




* **Main risks:**
* **Extremely high Fame Risk:** large models know this repo's routes and implementation by heart.


* **Public API trap:** frontend often hard-codes `[https://api.realworld.io](https://api.realworld.io)` by default. Without environment-variable changes, it appears successfully deployed while connecting to an external server.





#### C2: RealWorld Vue 3 + FastAPI (Python)

* **Frontend**: `[https://github.com/mutoe/vue3-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/mutoe/vue3-realworld-example-app)`
* **Backend**: `[https://github.com/nsidnev/fastapi-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/nsidnev/fastapi-realworld-example-app)`
* **Initial licence and maintenance:** MIT. Modern code (Vite + Pinia; Python 3.10+ Async FastAPI + SQLAlchemy).
* **Docker/Compose and acceptance leads:**
* Complete backend `docker-compose.yml` (App + PostgreSQL + database migration scripts).
* Standard OpenAPI/Swagger documentation endpoint, compatible with RealWorld automated API tests.


* **Main risks:**
* Unless frontend compile-time environment variables (Vite `VITE_API_URL`) are injected dynamically during Nginx image build, the runtime container cannot dynamically redirect the API.
* Moderate Fame Risk, lower than Node/React.



#### C3: RealWorld SvelteKit + Go (Gin)

* **Frontend**: `[https://github.com/sveltejs/realworld](https://github.com/sveltejs/realworld)`
* **Backend**: `[https://github.com/gothinkster/golang-gin-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/gothinkster/golang-gin-realworld-example-app)`
* **Initial licence and maintenance:** MIT. Go and the official Svelte ecosystem; very small build artefacts.
* **Docker/Compose and acceptance leads:**
* Backend single binary or lightweight Alpine/Scratch container, builds in seconds with very low Token and memory use.
* Standard REST interface, fully matching RealWorld acceptance.




* **Main risks:**
* SvelteKit mixed SSR/client SPA modes can cause reverse-proxy 502 if container port mapping is wrong.
* Few dependencies may fail to expose deeper package-dependency debugging conflicts.



#### C4: Vikunja (full-featured real open-source application outside RealWorld)

* **Frontend**: `https://kolaente.dev/vikunja/frontend` (GitHub mirror: `go-vikunja/frontend`)
* **Backend**: `https://kolaente.dev/vikunja/api` (GitHub mirror: `go-vikunja/api`)
* **Initial licence and maintenance:** AGPL-3.0 (note: deployment as a verification Target does not trigger source-code contagion, but record it). Frequent active maintenance.
* **Docker/Compose and acceptance leads:**
* Official industrial-grade Docker Compose configuration, naturally supporting separated frontend/backend networking.
* Built-in JWT accounts and optional OpenID Connect (can model third-party Auth without requiring it).


* **Main risks:**
* More complex than RealWorld (optional email and Redis cache, among others); strict initial environment-variable requirements.
* Very low model code familiarity (low Fame Risk), a real test of bare-AI deployment.



#### C5: RealWorld Angular + Java Spring Boot 3

* **Frontend**: `[https://github.com/gothinkster/angular-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/gothinkster/angular-realworld-example-app)`
* **Backend**: `[https://github.com/gothinkster/spring-boot-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/gothinkster/spring-boot-realworld-example-app)`
* **Initial licence and maintenance:** MIT. Enterprise structure, upgraded to Spring Boot 3 / Java 17+.
* **Docker/Compose and acceptance leads:**
* Maven/Gradle build containers and Compose orchestration.


* **Main risks:**
* **High memory/resource cost:** Spring Boot cold start and Maven builds need significant memory and CPU; lightweight VMs such as e2-medium easily time out or stall.
* Very long build logs waste AI tuning Token context.



---

### 4. 2–3 candidates recommended for `CORE_06-0a` local screening

1. **First Dev Workload choice (Run A / B / C): C2 (Vue 3 + FastAPI + PostgreSQL)**

* **Reason:** clean code, moderate weight. FastAPI's quality Swagger and automated-test interfaces, combined with Python and a modern frontend, form a typical architecture that current AI handles well but can mishandle through ‘environment-variable passing and reverse-proxy networking’; suitable for testing state-machine and verification discipline.




2. **First Holdout Workload choice (Run H blind test): C3 (SvelteKit + Go Gin)**

* **Reason:** fully heterogeneous versus Dev (Go + SvelteKit versus Python + Vue), but identical interface contracts (RealWorld), allowing test-script reuse without rewriting. Fast builds allow a clean test of WatchOver generalisation across stacks.




3. **Alternative (real project outside RealWorld): C4 (Vikunja)**
* **Reason:** if the Human Operator strongly objects to RealWorld Fame Risk (memorised answers), Vikunja is the most mature genuinely separated frontend/backend candidate, with optional OIDC.



---

### 5. Unknowns still requiring `CORE_06-0a` local verification

The local Executor screening dispatch must check these unverified facts:

1. **Default public-API trap:** inspect frontend `src/` for hard-coded `[https://api.realworld.io](https://api.realworld.io)` or third-party domains and whether missing environment variables silently fall back to an external Demo API.


2. **Local Docker cold-build success:** can `docker compose build` succeed in one go without network retrieval of private packages? Are NPM / PyPI dependencies deprecated or defunct?


3. **Real objective acceptance connectivity:** can official Newman/Postman tests (or project-specific scripts) run against the target Backend in a local single-container environment and output a quantitative pass rate?


4. **CORS defaults:** does the backend allow any Origin by default, or require the frontend's real domain (`https://baseline.<EXPERIMENT_DOMAIN>`) explicitly in startup parameters? This tests AI environment configuration.

### Unknowns local screening must confirm

I will not guess these from public README material: **whether a fresh clone truly builds/runs in one attempt; actual repo size/token footprint; hidden hard-coded localhost/public API; Docker build success; genuinely passing tests; code changes needed for Google/Keycloak redirect URI at <EXPERIMENT_DOMAIN>; AI instruction files; whether GitHub Actions is CI only or real deployment; number of secret requirements; actual licence content at the target commit.**

In particular, **‘amount of code modification’ should be a hard observation in 0a**. If a workload needs changes to a dozen or more business files for GCP, the experiment measures porting ability rather than WatchOver.

---

### I support your ‘three-workload’ experiment, but §7 needs a formal change

Your idea has a clear advantage over the current roadmap.

Current roadmap:

**One dev workload: Bare A → WatchOver B → Guarded C; then one holdout H.** [Historical client citation 25; target unavailable in this captured record]

Your proposal:

**Workload 1: fully blind Bare AI, discovering real pain points.
Workload 2: controlled Bare versus initial WatchOver comparison on the same new workload.
Workload 3: final verification on an unseen workload after WatchOver is finalised.**

This is actually **cleaner methodologically**.

The current design has a potential bias: observe Bare AI stumble on Workload 1, design WatchOver for those failures, then return to **the same workload** for B. Even a clearly better B may partly reflect workload overfitting.

Your design separates **discovery workload** and **evaluation workload**:

`W1 discovery → design WatchOver → W2 controlled A/B → finalize → W3 holdout`

W2 becomes the actual primary efficacy test; W3 tests generalisation / final holdout.

My one firm requirement: **W2 must run both Bare and WatchOver, with exactly the same goal text, model/tier, permissions, DNS method and acceptance checklist.** Do not compare W1 Bare numbers directly with W2 WatchOver numbers; workload itself would be a confounder.

The cost is clear: one extra cloud run, more money and time. Within USD 280 credit and hard 20 October teardown, I think Council cross-review is worthwhile, rather than quietly changing the roadmap today. The current experiment is fixed in §7; if all three agree, patch it explicitly, instead of the Executor discovering the change only during execution.
